title: Bathroom Problems
protagonist: Will Thomason, father of eight and head of the household
primary_metric: total 'useful bathroom minutes' delivered to the family each morning -- the sum, across all eight family members, of each person's assigned time capped at their own real stated need (so a surplus given to someone who didn't need it doesn't count) -- comparing a flat equal-rotation schedule (Option A) against a needs-weighted proportional schedule (Option B)

options.A: Set a fixed rotating schedule -- every family member gets an identical time slot each morning, rotating weekly so no one is stuck with the worst slot long-term
options.B: Set a needs-weighted schedule -- slot order and length prioritized by who has the earliest fixed commitment each morning, even if it isn't equal

legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y2/Session 3/Bathroom Problems/Case Study_ Bathroom Problems.docx + Guide Notes.docx) is a real Acton Academy/Heroes Academy case about the Thomason family of eight sharing one working bathroom after a flood. The family roster, ages, individually tracked bathroom-activity times, 'needs to leave the house by' times (Appendix A), the master bathroom's fixtures and water-usage data including the water heater's First Hour Rating (Appendix C), the flood backstory, the three house sharing-rules (Will-and-Marta may share; no one else in the bathroom during a shower; the daily 5-minute family devotional), and Thomas's 6:45 AM wake time next to the master bathroom are all preserved directly from the source, not invented. The original dilemma had ZERO named options -- it was an open scheduling task for a rotating, unnamed protagonist ('You are a ___ [a member of the Thomason family chosen during the case study launch]. Create a schedule...'). Per cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md's 'bathroom-problems' entry (re-framed from an original RETIRE recommendation), this conversion locks a genuine, constructed binary in the fairness-vs-efficiency shape: Option A (fixed equal rotating slots) vs. Option B (needs-weighted slots by leave-time urgency) -- the same pattern as the already-published food-rationing case's equal-vs-need binary. What this conversion adds, since the locked options did not exist in the source: (a) a fixed, single named protagonist, Will Thomason -- the source left the protagonist open-ended ('any family member'), but SPEC.md section 1.4 requires one named person; Will is the parent with the stated authority and accountability for building the schedule (he calls the family meeting and does the scheduling with Marta), which is the most SPEC-defensible fixed choice while the case still notes any family member's shoes could be used live, matching the source's original flexibility; (b) a fully worked, computable version of both locked options, built entirely from the real Appendix A/C data -- a shared 70-minute morning window derived from the real given facts (Thomas's 6:45 AM wake time + the daily devotional + Appendix A's own latest leave-by time), a flat-equal allocation for Option A, and a proportional needs-weighted allocation for Option B, compared on a genuinely balanced 'useful minutes delivered' metric (10.24% margin, well inside SPEC section 2's 20% cap); (c) one disclosed Modeling Assumption (MA1, case.md) about exactly when the devotional happens, since the source states only that it happens 'before anyone leaves the house' without fixing a time; (d) two real-world grounding citations (S2, S3) for the water heater First Hour Rating concept and typical U.S. showerhead flow rates, added as context since the case's own numeric claims (Appendix A/C) are the family's own given scenario data, not independently-verifiable real-world facts requiring external sourcing -- the same treatment food-rationing gave its own given boat-inventory data. The Twist (Guide Notes.docx: Grandma Polly and Grandpa Ben arrive with their suitcases to help with repairs) is preserved directly from the original source and quantified for this conversion in FACILITATOR.md/sensitivity_model.py's evaluate_twist() (two more adults added to the household, each needing bathroom time -- a disclosed facilitator-side estimate, MA2, not shown in case.md since the Twist is withheld until the discussion). The Guide Notes' five-anchor structure is reformatted to this pipeline's format without altering its real content or discussion questions; no full timed Socratic plan existed in the source, so one is authored fresh in FACILITATOR.md per SPEC.md section 7.3.

balance.argument_a: The Round-Robin is procedurally simple and unimpeachably fair in the sense that matters most to a room full of teenagers: nobody is ever permanently stuck with the worst position. Every family member gets the exact same 8.75-minute slot, and next week the person who went last this week goes first. It requires no judgment calls about whose need is 'more real,' and it is trivial to enforce without an argument breaking out every morning about whose hair actually takes 36 minutes. This isn't just a procedural nicety: the Priority Line's own turn-order rule (earliest leave-by time first, ties broken by lower total need) has no rotation at all -- it produces the exact same order every single day. Under it, Marta is permanently last (latest leave-by time, and the highest remaining need in that tier gets pushed to the back of it), which means her turn ends at exactly 8:00:00 -- her own leave-by time, with zero buffer -- and by the time she starts, cumulative hot-water usage has already passed the 28-minute First Hour Rating limit (Appendix C/D3), so she showers in fully cold water every morning. The Round-Robin's rotating order means no one is ever permanently in that position two weeks running.
balance.argument_b: The Priority Line delivers 70.0 useful minutes to the family instead of 63.5 -- the Round-Robin wastes 6.5 minutes/day on family members like Thomas and George who don't need their full flat slot, while badly shortchanging Heather (8.75 of her stated 57) and Marta (8.75 of her stated 47). Under the Priority Line, every single family member gets exactly the same 30.8% of their own real need met -- arguably a much more meaningful definition of 'equal' than an equal number of raw minutes that means something completely different to an 11-year-old (George, who needs 8) than to a 16-year-old getting ready for school (Heather, who needs 57).
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric = 'useful minutes delivered,' the sum across all 8 family members of min(their assigned slot, their real stated need). Option A (flat 70/8 = 8.75 min/person): useful = 63.5 min. Option B (proportional share of 70 min by need, out of 227 total minutes needed): useful = 70.0 min (always the full window, since proportional allocation is always below 100% of anyone's real need). Margin = (70.0 - 63.5) / 63.5 = 10.24%.

modeling_assumptions.text: The five-minute family devotional happens first thing every morning, right when Thomas wakes (6:45-6:50 AM), before any individual bathroom turns begin -- setting the shared window's start time. The source states only that the devotional happens 'before anyone leaves the house,' not exactly when.

sensitivity_note: The 10.24% margin is real but not extremely robust -- it is sensitive to Modeling Assumption MA1 (case.md), the case author's placement of the shared devotional at the very start of the morning. A +/-50% flex of the resulting shared-window figure (case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5, sensitivity_model.py FLEX=['window_minutes']) moves the margin between roughly 4% and 17%, but never flips which option wins -- Option B (needs-weighted) stays ahead across the full flex range tested. See sensitivity_model.py for the worked sweep.

cohort_bands.note: Anchors 2-3 run as written; the room splits into a 'simple and equal' faction and an 'efficient but unequal' faction before the Twist forces a recompute with two more people sharing the same window.

Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; D5's two visual displays are worked as one shared example instead of every Hero building both independently; the 'deep conflict' threads (equal-treatment vs. efficiency; role-based authority; who bears the cost of scarcity) drop to one thread instead of two or three; total runtime shortens proportionally.

There is no vote to take, so Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position instead of a stand/sit vote; the guide plays devil's advocate directly rather than cold-calling; the twist still lands but 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse, and why.'
